utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I understand there are certain technical difficulties this morning with the equipment, but essentially that is confined to the transcript on e-court. The transcript exists in the normal form, and e-court will handle the exhibits. So there is no reason why we cannot continue. Mr. Visnjic, who is your next witness? Oh, sorry, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. The next witness is Radomir Gojovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Gojovic. Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Witness answered through interpreter].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You will now be examined by Mr. Sepenuk on behalf of Mr. Ojdanic. Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Good morning, General Gojovic.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Sir, what is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: I am a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And where do you practice?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: In Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's Note: Could Mr. Sepenuk please switch off his mic when the witness is mic'ing his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Are you a formerly a member of the Yugoslav Army?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And how long did you serve in the Yugoslav Army?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: From 1963 until 2001, for 40 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And you retired in 2001; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And what was your rank at retirement?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Major general.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Now, General, would you briefly describe your career in the army and also your military legal career.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: I completed the school for non-commissioned officers in the infantry in Sarajevo. Then I graduated from the high school and the school of law in Sarajevo. And for ten years, from 1961 to 1971, I was the commander of the mortar platoon and the recoilless rifle platoon. I was a troop commander. After I completed the law school, I was transferred to the legal service. That was in 1971. And from that time on, I was a legal profession. I worked in the legal judiciary for 30 years -- in the military legal judiciary for 30 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And did that include the -- being the former president of the military court in Belgrade from 1994 to 1999?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And on April 16th, 1999, is it true that you were appointed chief of the legal department of the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Who appointed you to that position?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: I was appointed by the President of the Republic at that time, and that was Slobodan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And before you were appointed to that position, did you meet with General Ojdanic, and if so, tell us what was said at that time.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was sometime on the 14th or the 15th of April. I was -- got a phone call from General Ojdanic. That was in the evening. And he told me that he should have an interview with me about some -- he should talk to me about some status-related issues and he asked me whether I agreed, and I said yes. The next day he came to the court and he told me about Milosevic -- President Milosevic's position, that President Milosevic had asked him to find some person to appoint to that post in order to improve the operation of military courts in wartime. He then told me that he talked to the president of the supreme military court and the supreme military prosecutor, asking them who could be professional enough to be appointed to that post, who had proper -- appropriate experience, and they gave him my name. I agreed to take that post, because I had already been at all the posts in the military judiciary. I was the deputy military prosecutor, the military prosecutor. I was a judge, a military judge. I was the president of the lower military court. And I agreed to take that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Was there any discussion at that time with General Ojdanic about whether the legal system was functioning well or not? And if so, what was that conversation?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, all military courts in wartime and all military prosecutors offices had already been set up. There had been some organisational difficulties at the outset in light of the fact that this was the first time for such courts to be set up. They had not functioned. They did not in fact exist from 1947, the end of the Second World War. So a great deal of experience was needed. Some problems had been encountered. And it was necessary to reorganise them and to make them more efficient, more efficient that -- than there had been up until that time. That's what we talked about.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, General, would you give us briefly an overview of the laws, rules, and regulations that apply during 1998 and 1999 regarding observance of international humanitarian law by members of the army. Just a brief overview, if you would.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Until the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, in Article 16 it is envisaged that all international treaties ratified by the parliament and published in accordance with the law and norms of international law apply, and they are an integral part of the internal legal system of Yugoslavia. That includes all the Geneva Conventions, all the protocols. So this is the basic provision in the Constitution. On the basis of that provision in the Constitution, the Law on Defence also envisages -- or rather, there is a provision in Article 19 of the Law on Defence stipulating that all personnel of the -- of the military in combat are duty-bound to abide by the Rules of International Law of law and other rules about the humane treatment of prisoners of war and the civilian population. In the law on the army of Yugoslavia - I think that is Article 31 - it is also stipulated that the military personnel in the course of executing their combat missions are entitled to use firearms in accordance with the rules of engagement, and the rules of engagement provide for the proper use of weapons in combat. These are the basic legal provisions. And there was also the instruction on the application of the international law of war in armed conflict. It was systematised and edited, revised in 1988. There was also an order of the President of the Republic on the application of this -- these laws in the army of Yugoslavia, and this is in fact still in force.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I want to go over with you again very briefly some other rules and regulations applicable in this area, and for that we're going to turn to Defence Exhibit 3D1110. And we have examined all of these rules and regulations before together, have we not?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And I'd first like to direct you to tab 2 of that exhibit, 3D1110, and that's at -- at 3D110172 in the English and 3D110036 in B/C/S. Do you -- do you recognise that, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: These are the rules. This is a brochure, "Rules on the application of the rules of international law of war." And they contain those provisions that I talked about a little while ago. So this was a hard-back brochure, and every unit at a certain level has this booklet in its possession. It has to be in the library.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And who --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And by the way, Your Honours, I notice the English version is not up, but it is the regulations on the application of international laws of war in the armed forces of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And I notice it's dated 1988. Were these rules and regulations applicable in 1998 and 1999? And if so, why were they applicable? How did they become applicable if they're dated 1988?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: They were applicable at that time too, and they are in force right now, because they contain all the Geneva Conventions, the 1947 Geneva Conventions and all the additional protocols and all the other -- other rules of international law of war and customs that are generally accepted. This booklet was published in 1988. That was when it was edited and revised and adapted to the actual needs. Nothing changed in the meantime. So the fact that it bears the date of 1988 doesn't mean much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes. But I asked you a specific question: Why is the 1988 rules applicable in 1998 and 1999, and whether the Constitution has anything to do with that.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the Constitution is the foundation for that, because it envisages that all the international regulations are to be applied and they are part of the internal legal system. So that is the foundation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now I'd like you to look at tab 3, which is the rules of combat for soldiers, and it's 3D110258 in the English and 3D110256 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I hope that's a mistake. 110258, Mr. Sepenuk. That can't be right. I hope.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Well, it's -- excuse me. It's 3D11-0258 in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: 11 dash?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes. That's the way it's numbered on my copy, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, this is the e-court page number?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, sorry. Sorry. What is the exhibit number, then?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: The exhibit number is 3D1110.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Still part of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, we have 18 or 19 tabs on this. So, again the English is at 3D11-0258, and there it is on the screen. And the B/C/S is 3D11-0256. Is it possible to put that up at the same time? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: General, you've seen these rules before, have you not, sir?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: What are they and who were they distributed to?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: The rules of conduct for soldiers, this is a small laminated leaflet that contains the most salient provisions of the international law of war. That is adapted to soldiers to use them in combat. This provides how a soldier should comport himself in combat, that they may fire only at other soldiers, that they should abide by the rules of the international law of war, that they should protect the civilian population, how to treat the wounded, in the battlefield, the wounded enemy, the wounded prisoners, and also how to treat property, to use only the combat warfare that is necessary to carry out the mission and not to use excessive force. So these are just the general rules that every soldier had to carry with him. This is a pocket-size leaflet and every soldier had it with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Was it one of those laminated leaflets that you -- small laminated leaflets that you can carry in your pocket?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's laminated. There are just two pages, so it is impervious to humidity and to water.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And now I'd like to turn to tab 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sepenuk, is this the -- the document that we've heard of 1300 copies being distributed?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I think there was some testimony, but the short of it, Your Honour, as I understand it - and that's one of the reasons General Gojovic is here - is that every single soldier received a copy of this. I forget the specifics of the 1300 copies, but I think there'll be other evidence, if there not already has been other evidence, that every soldier received a copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Gojovic, how did every soldier come into possession of a copy of this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was printed, and just as every soldier is issued weapons and other equipment, they were also given this small leaflet. So this is nothing new. And the cost was negligible. If you can supply every soldier with all the equipment they need, you could give him those two pieces of paper too. And the soldier has it in his kit. When a soldier is mobilised, when she's issued weapons and other equipment, he get this is leaflet, "Rules of conduct for soldiers in combat."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And now I'd like to turn to handout 4, which is handbook for VG members engaged in areas affected by sabotage and terrorist activities from June 1998. And that's in the English at 3D11-0271.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And you're familiar with that document, are you not, sir?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And just very briefly tell -- it's a -- tell the Trial Chamber what it provided for. Very briefly.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, just as there was the rules of conduct of soldiers in combat, there was an analogous document dealing with the way in which soldiers should comport themselves in the fight against the terrorists in Kosovo and Metohija. So all the rules were incorporated in it, but there were some other rules as to how to treat members of terrorist groups if they were captured. They were to be treated in the same manner, although they did not have the status of prisoners of war. They should be treated as if they were prisoner of wars and they should be handed over to the competent organs in order to be prosecuted, because terrorism is a crime. So this was adapted to this particular situation in fighting against terrorist groups. So it was just slightly modified and some new provisions were included about fighting terrorist groups and infiltrated sabotage groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: In your knowledge, General, who received a copy of this handbook?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: These handbooks were distributed to the soldiers who were engaged in fighting terrorist groups, so just them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: All right. Now I'd like to turn again very briefly to tab 5, which is a resume of the four Geneva Conventions and protocols. And we have it, I think, Your Honours, only in B/C/S. I don't really want to spend much time on it. I'll simply ask the general what was that document and who was it distributed to, to your knowledge? For the record, it's at 3D11-0279. You know what I'm talking about, General, do you not?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Just tell us -- just tell us again, very briefly, what it was. And if you know, who was it distributed to.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: This handbook contains just a brief outline of all the Geneva Conventions from 1947 and the additional protocols, just the briefest outline of the contents, all unit commanders from platoon commander, company commander and upwards, they had the handbook with them. So we're talking about commander -- unit commanders, "komandiri."

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you. And finally on this subject, if you would look at tab 6, which is the Yugoslav Army Supreme Command Staff fundamentals of the laws of war, a summary for officers, at 3D11-0309 in the English. 3D11-0294 in the B/C/S. And you're familiar with this document, General? We don't have the B/C/S up yet.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: I know about this document, but I can't see it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes. It's -- now it's up, I believe. "Fundamentals of the law of war." Do you recognise that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's it; although, I don't see the rest of the text. That's the fundamentals of the law of war. This is just a basic principles of the law of war, basic concepts, some explanations, and unit commanders also had this document. The soldiers were not issued that. They didn't need that. They had this and the summary of the Geneva Conventions from 1947 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, aside from what you've talked about, the Constitution, Rules of Defence, rules of the army, and these other provisions we've talked about, please tell us the specific laws prohibiting the commission of war crimes and the specific law prohibiting murder and multiple murder in both in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia Criminal Code and the Serbian Criminal Code.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to the regulations that we've already discussed, in the Criminal Code of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia there is a chapter containing crimes -- or rather, where persons who commit war crimes during wartime are sanctioned. A number of different crimes: Crime against -- war crime against civilian population, war crime against prisoners and wounded, genocide. This is all stipulated in the Criminal Code. Every perpetrator is prosecuted and tried.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I want to focus on war crimes against the -- the civilian population. What article is that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: That is mentioned in Article 142 of the Criminal Code of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And what is the minimum and maximum sentences pertaining to that article?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: The minimum sentence is five years in prison and the maximum sentence is twenty years in prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Prior to -- when did the 20-year maximum go into effect?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was up to the court. It depended on the manner in which the crime was committed, the seriousness of the crime, and the threat to the society. If a person ordered the commission of such a crime and if the civilian population sustained suffering for no reason, then this maximum sentence would apply.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: But, again, the maximum sentence was 20 years; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Now, what was the article in the Serbian code which covered murder and multiple murder?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: The Criminal Code of Serbia has Article 1 -- Article 47, several forms of homicide, paragraph 1 is just ordinary murder, one person is killed; and if you have several persons killed, then it's multiple murder, at least ten years, that's the sentence for this kind of murder, or even death penalty. In the federal law, the death penalty was abolished, but in the Criminal Code of the Republic, it -- the death penalty existed up until 2005, when the Criminal Code was finally amended.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So the short of it is, General, that the penalties for the crime of murder are more severe than the penalties for the Article 142 war crimes. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. Now, we've talked about the rules, the regulations, the laws prohibiting, commission of crimes. Now tell us about the judicial system that was set up during the war to prosecute crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Well, I apologise interfering. Forgive me, please. Now, I just wanted to clarify whether the Criminal Code of Serbia was applicable to the armed forces or was it applicable generally as a corpus juris for everybody in that area. Did it apply exclusively for the army, like the case of Article 142 of the Criminal Code of FRY. I mean, how -- how these both could be brought together. Because otherwise there'll be a principle of -- of double jeopardy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: General, do you understand His Honour's question?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: I understood the question. It's a unified, single law or legal system, and it applies to all members, that is, all perpetrators of that crime, all citizens, regardless of whether they are civilians or members of the army. However, military courts only had jurisdiction over members of the army. If the perpetrator was a civilian, then the civilian court would deal with it. So there would be no double jeopardy, no two trials. There's only one court trying this crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: So a person of the army, if he committed several murders, will he be tried under Article 142 or will he be tried under the Criminal Code of Serbia and then what will be the forum?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For someone to be held liable under Article 142 of the Criminal Code of the FRY, if that was a military commander who ordered that crime to be committed, to his underlings or if it was a member of the army, a subordinate member of the army they would answer under Article 142 of the Federal law. However, prosecutors opted during the wartime in cases when this crime was not the result of an order but something done on an individual's own initiative, they opted to act under the republican law, because the republican law envisaged a more severe punishment. In the course of trials, Defence counsel usually made motions that were successful in many cases that the crime be tried under Article 142, because it was, if I may put it that way, more lenient. If those murders or multiple murders were committed during war operations or combat against civilians, against the wounded in wartime.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Is that satisfactory, Your Honour? Is that satisfactory?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I think there's still a bit of a confusion, because -- will the penal law applicable to everybody apply to the soldiers who committed murder, let's say of their own initiative, rather than by the directions of a commander, what will happen? And will it be a military court or ordinary court? I mean, this is still something. But anyway, you can kindly help us later on, Mr. Sepenuk. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just for the transcript, Mr. Sepenuk, these questions are posed by Judge Chowhan and not by Judge Kamenova.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Now, General, tell us about the judicial system that was set up during the war to prosecute crimes.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: With a proclamation of the state of war on the 26th of March, the chief of General Staff issued an order in keeping with the state of war that military courts in wartime and military prosecutors in wartime be established. On the basis of that, the peacetime military courts and military prosecution offices seized their [Realtime transcript read in error "washing"] work, and work proceeded to establish military courts and military prosecution offices. They were formed as part of commands of individual units. In total, 20 first-instance courts and 20 first-instance prosecutor's offices were established as part of commands of units.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: General, let me just interrupt you for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just before you do, Mr. Sepenuk, we can't allow to go unnoticed a reference to the military judiciary and prosecution seizing their washing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Seized their washing, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You may be able to help us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I'm sure Mr. Cepic can enlighten us.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I believe, Your Honour, there are some more errors in transcript. First of all, I found on the two places that the witness mentioned 1949 in relation to Geneva Conventions, but in transcript it is 1947. That is first. Secondly, page 12, line 12. Defence counsel usually made motions that were successful. I think that witness did not say as in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Can you help us with the washing?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I think that Mr. Sepenuk is in charge right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Back to you, Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: We could go back to it right now, Your Honour, if you'd like. Otherwise, I'll continue on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry I mentioned it, but it seemed to brighten up a Monday morning -- Tuesday morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm also a day behind. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: General, excuse me for interrupting, but I wanted to just get back a little bit in terms of how many military court there is were in peacetime. Just tell us that briefly. Military courts in peacetime. How many were there and where did they sit?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: In peacetime, there were three first-instance military courts: One in Belgrade, one in Nis, and one in Podgorica, there were also three peacetime prosecutor's offices in these locations. There was also a supreme military court and a supreme military prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Based both in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Now, after the war, how many military courts were established? I think you said 20. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Correct, 20 first-instance military courts, and the same number of prosecutor's offices. There was also a supreme military court and supreme military prosecutor's office. Plus they had their own sections each, and they were subordinate to army commands. There were three sections each, three sections of both organs that dealt with appeals. So in total, there were 24 courts and 24 prosecutor's offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And these 20 Trial Courts, could you just reel off from memory - I hope you can do that - some of the locations where they were at.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: I know all the locations. The trial military courts were set up annexed to army commands, the 1st, 2nd, and 3rd armies, that is, Belgrade, Nis, and Podgorica. They were also form within corps commands, Belgrade, Nis, Podgorica, Uzice, and others, and as part of military districts commands and division commands. There was one division as well as -- as part of the Navy and air force and air defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And how about defence lawyers? Were there provisions for defence lawyers and if so, what were they? Very briefly.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: According to establishment, there was a loophole earlier. There was no establishment first of Defence counsel. When I came to my position, I noticed this lacuna. So later on we proceeded to organise defence free of charge and Defence counsel were at the disposal of every court to be appointed, to be assigned as Defence counsel, if necessary. So that element was also included in the judiciary.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And were rules of organisation and procedure enacted for both military courts and military prosecutors? Just "yes" or "no."

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And I'd like you to --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, Your Honours, and with the permission of -- or at least the concurrence of the Prosecution, tabs, 8, 9, 10, and 11 represent the Rules of Procedure of military courts and military prosecutors. And I'd simply like to mention that to Your Honours. It's listed in 65 ter. And just for the record, tab 8 is the organization and work of the military prosecutor and that's at 3D11-0329 this is again 3D1110. Tab 9 is the law on military courts, 3D11-0337. Tab 10 is the application of law of criminal procedure during a state of war, 3D11-0346. And tab 11, 3D0355, Proma [phoen] getting the law on the military prosecutor. And I think we'll just move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, you accept these -- these appear to be what they're said to be?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Move on, Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Now after assuming your duties as chief of the General Staff's legal department on April 16th, 1999, was there in your opinion, a sufficient number of judges and prosecutors to do an adequate job?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: I noted immediately that the number of judges or prosecutors was insufficient. They were really minimal in number and inadequate. That is one thing. And the second thing is that according to the wartime assignment, although candidates met all the requirements, they passed the bar exam and had a law degree, the persons appointed to such posts had no previous experiences, judges or prosecutors. So one of the first things to do was to replace those people by persons who had previously worked in the judiciary, mainly from district courts, because they had experienced personnel, so that at my proposal the personnel was replaced in order to have the work done as efficiently and as professionally as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So a number of new judges and prosecutors were appointed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And are -- are the specific numbers reflected in tab 12 of Exhibit 3D1110 at 3D11-0370?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: There were 155 judges in total and 92 prosecutors, and the newly appointed ones were 125 in number. They were promoted to be officers because military prosecutors and judges have to be officers. So they were given the status of reserve officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: 125 of them, therefore, were appointed within a very short period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And again, Your Honours, the specifics are reflected in tab 12 under -- at the page I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Now, having set up a system of military courts, military prosecutors, Defence lawyers, as you've testified, were there rules and procedure in place for those courts to operate? And you can just answer "yes" or "no" to that.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And as the war progressed and the number of crimes increased, did you see a need to improve the system?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And did you personally draft guidelines to improve the functioning of the system?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And are those guidelines reflected in tab 13 of Defence Exhibit 3D1110? "Yes" or "no"?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, this is at 3D11-0380 in the English. I'm just going to pass on. I just want the panel to be aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Now, during the war, was part of your job to monitor the work of the military courts in prosecuting crimes?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And to that end, did you visit military prosecutor's offices and military courts to see how they operated?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And very briefly, tell us about that. How many offices did you visit?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: I toured all the military courts and military prosecutor's offices during their war; that is, 24 in total.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Twenty-four courts and twenty-four prosecutor's offices, and that is a total of forty-eight.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And when you toured these military courts and prosecutor's offices during the war, what were some of the physical problems, if any, that you noticed, some of the physical problems and difficulties of operating the court system? Just tell us briefly about that.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Of course there were some difficulties. When I say "of course," it's because we were under the conditions of war. There were daily air strikes by the forces of NATO. They flew over the entire territory of the former Republic of Yugoslavia. There were frequent air alerts and military prosecutors had to move frequently from their locations. And apart from that, communication with parties was made significantly more difficult because the accused or suspects were supposed to appear before the court. That created difficulties in the safety of movement and the safety of movement of investigators and judges, especially in the area of Kosovo and Metohija, because in addition to air strikes on that territory, it was dangerous to move across that terrain in view of the danger posed by terrorist forces in and around settlements. So there were significant difficulties in communicating with parties. In addition to that, units moved even more often than the courts did, so that the work of prosecutors and judges was really very difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: How about your office? Did you have to move?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: I had to relocate with my department and my personnel. While I was there in that position, we moved three times, and the location itself changed to -- two to three times. So we moved in total five or six times. That requires every time re-establishing communications, setting up in a new place, and all the military organisations moved as well, so we had to find each other again every time in order to be able to communicate.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Now, General, after you'd been on the job for about a month, did you write a report about the military judicial organs to that point, their functioning to that point?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And I want to direct your attention to 3D1110, tab 15. I'm going to ask you if that's the report that you wrote. It's in e-court in English 3D11-0404; in B/C/S, 3D11-0398.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, if -- if I may, I believe this document is already in Exhibit P2826, which was admitted on the 28th of March. So for the sake of efficiency, I would prefer that we refer to it by that number, as it's already been used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Well, the thing is it's in e-court specifically under pagination, there's 18 different tabs. And I have all my -- questions keyed to the e-court numbers for 3D1110, so I don't think it would be -- it shouldn't be a particular problem for Mr. Hannis to follow this. I always like to comply with anything that Mr. Hannis says, but I think this one is, you know, pretty reasonable on our part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What you'll find, Mr. Hannis is that correct P2826 is a number that will be used eventually, but now that we know the two are identical, then for the purpose of presentation at this stage, I think it's acceptable for Mr. Sepenuk to proceed the way he's proceeding.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour. I don't have a problem following. But for the sake of the record at the end of the case. And while I'm up, I guess I should follow to go or three others in this sequence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It is helpful if you do that, so that we don't lose sight of the identity between two exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Tab 14 wasn't mentioned, but what is P2825. Tab 16 is P953. Tab 17 is P954. Tab 18A is P955.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And some of these, like 954 and 955, Your Honours, we did refer to in our 65 ter summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Now, General, do we have that up on the ... So you see the report that you wrote on the left there and on the right it's in English; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. Now, first let's get the dates straight. At the beginning of the report, it says September 12th, 1999. And that flat out is wrong; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: That's wrong. On the back side, on the last page, there is an authentic date. This one is an error.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And what is the authentic date?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: That is when you actually wrote this report; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And who was the report submitted to?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: That report was intended for the Supreme Command Staff, and I submitted it to the Department for Mobilisation and Reinforcement that forwarded it to the Supreme Command Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. Can we turn to section 2.3 of the report, 3D11-0405 in English, and 3D11-0399 in B/C/S. And could you scroll up a bit on the English to -- where it says 2.3. And if you would blow up 2.3, I'd be grateful. Do you see section 2.3, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: All right. Now, the first paragraph of that - and I'll read it. You follow in the B/C/S and make sure that I'm reading it correctly and getting the full gist of the translation - "It was assessed that the volume and complexity of the tasks faced by military judicial organs in this strategic group was too great a load for the existing establishment, and after making adjustments and overcoming initial difficulties, the military organs have become fully operational." Is that -- did I read that correctly? Is that what it says in the B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Essentially, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. Now, that was your opinion, correct, that the military judicial organs have become fully operational? Was that your opinion?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And throughout the remainder of your time as the chief of the legal department of the General Staff, did you ever change that opinion?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: All right. Now, go to the next paragraph. It says: "The first organ -- the first-instance organs attached to the command of the third army, the Nis Corps and Nis military District have proved extremely efficient, unlike the judicial organs attached to the command of the military district in Nis." First I want to ask you: Is there an error in that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: A small error. It's a slip. The last one should be "the military district in Pristina," not Nis. Because the military district in Nis operated well and there were certain deficiencies and weaknesses in the operation of the military district in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Can you be more specific? What were those problems? What were the problems in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I -- I noted a moment ago that there were difficulties in Pristina because intensive fighting went on there, so that the military court attached to the command of the military district in Pristina did not really have the right conditions for -- for working well, because the conditions of movement, of prosecutors, witnesses and other parties was very difficult and they could not operate properly. Those were the objective reasons why they couldn't operate properly. And there were also difficulties with filling all the vacancies. Later on, when the staffing was complete, that improved a little, but there remained the organisational difficulties.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And is it fair to say that those difficulties remained pretty much throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Throughout the war, yes, because the circumstances didn't change. They did not improve.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you. And would you please turn to the third paragraph, where it says: "Military judicial organs attached to the Pristina Corps Command have encountered in their work very complex criminal cases that deal with serious crimes (terrorism, murder, robbery, theft, et cetera), which require the prosecutors and judges to have a high degree of expertise and experience." My question, General, is: How did you know about these crimes? How did you find out about them? What was your sources of information?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, my sources of information were reports of military courts and military prosecutor's offices that were submitted to the supreme military court and supreme military prosecutor's office, who in turn made available to me these reports about criminal cases and the criminal proceedings initiated as a result. I saw from those reports that we are facing very complex crime, that it is extremely complex work that requires indeed a high degree of expertise and experience on the part of military judges and prosecutors.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: All right. And you went on to say that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you move on, Mr. Sepenuk, Mr. Gojovic, what's the reference there to terrorism.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that relates to terrorist groups, ethnic Albanians that composed those terrorist groups. They abducted people in one occasion, the suspects and the witness who came to the court and on the way back to the unit three of them were abducted and their fate remains unknown.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The paragraph we're looking at, though, is dealing with the military judicial organs dealing with serious crimes and terrorism is given as one of the examples. Now, can you give me an example of a crime of terrorism that the military judicial organs were dealing with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Military courts during the war did not prosecute those cases. They merely registered those cases, but many of such cases were dealt with by the district courts, the civilian courts. Military courts did not prosecute those cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's possibly my misunderstanding of this, but I assume the military courts did not have jurisdiction over terrorists.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This crime is not in the exclusive jurisdiction of the military courts. It is in the jurisdiction of the district courts. But they were victims of those terrorist acts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you answer -- can you answer my question: Did the military courts have jurisdiction over terrorists? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. If they targeted military personnel and provided they got caught.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So that takes me back to my original question: What are you referring to in that paragraph when you talk about terrorism being one of the serious crimes that the military judicial organs were dealing with? Can you give me an example?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I've just given you an example. They faced those crimes, but they were not in a position to catch the perpetrators. I mentioned that three military servicemen who had come to the court were abducted. This is a crime. They were killed, but their fate -- they were probably killed, but their fate remains unknown. They're still missing. And abduction, an abduction -- every abduction is a terrorist act.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Would you just turn to the next page, which is 3D11-0406 in English and ... Okay. Do we have the English? 3D11-0406. And then 3D11-0400 in B/C/S. Okay. And if you just make 3 a little bit larger. Thank you. And do you notice, General, the paragraph that says "Number of cases"?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Would you just -- let me just read one sentence to you. It says: "Some 3897 persons have been indicted, 997 judgements have been pronounced, 2393 criminal cases have been closed, and 205 on-site investigations of destroyed buildings and other crimes have been carried out." There's other matters in that paragraph. I'm not going to get into them. It says: "Attachments 1 to 3." Was the basis for those figures an attachment that is in this case as tab 14 that we've previously discussed? You can answer that"yes" or "no."

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, for the record - and Mr. Hannis referred to this before - tab 14 is the list of convictions per category of persons, type of crime, and length of sentence as of 15 May 1999. And it's 3D11-0392.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Gojovic, when that paragraph refers to 2.393 criminal cases being closed, what -- what does "being closed" mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. The translation is not really very good. Case concluded? I don't know. Well, 7.800 criminal reports, requests for investigation filed against 2.911 persons.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down when reading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Gojovic -- Mr. Gojovic, just a moment. The interpreter can't follow you if you speak so quickly. I wonder if you could speak a little more slowly and deal with that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. I understand. I merely wanted to concentrate on what you asked me. 2.393 investigations that were completed. The investigating judge completes the investigation and then submits the file or the dossier to the military prosecutor's office. So after that, then you can have an indictment. And the reason why I was a little bit confused is because the term that I got back was "zakljuceni" not concluded. And then it says that 3.897 persons were indicted and that 997 judgements were pronounced and that 2.393 criminal cases were closed. If you -- if you add all that up, that means that the proceedings in those cases were actually completed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I'm still not understanding that, then, because I thought part of your answer there was to suggest that these 2.393 were not in fact completed. Are you saying they have been completed but there has been no judgement in these cases?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This figure, 2.393, this is about the work of the court. The court has to conduct and complete an investigation. The court completed a certain number of investigations, and it -- they have to deliver judgements. They -- once they deliver the first-instance judgement, the case is completed. And this is the figure that relates to this stage in the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't understand these figures, Mr. Sepenuk. If -- if they're of any significance to you, you'll need to have them clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I think that -- and I agree. It's -- it's certainly not very clear to me either. But we are going to go to another report of September which I think will clarify it, a later report with, I think, more accurate -- more meaningful figures. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I -- sorry to interrupt you, interrupting. But he -- the general is a lawyer as well. When we talk of a case being closed, that comes under -- under a technical heading; meaning that the case didn't proceed. And it was closed at its nascent stage or without any adjudicatory action in it. So this is where the confusion arises. Does he mean closure of a case after a judgement or does he mean closure of a case before a judgement? I mean, that would answer the question. I'm sorry, I'm talking of these number of cases here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once a stage in the proceedings is completed, that's what we're talking about. At this stage, we don't have a final judgement, because the appellate proceedings are still pending. So these are not cases that are closed in the sense that they have been put ad acta.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: A very simple question. Is question is: These cases which were mentioned were closed. Does it mean -- these 2393 cases. Were they closed after a judgement, after an adjudication, or were these collated prematurely before a judgement, before witnesses coming to testify? Because these were not proceedable, these were not tenable in law. This is the question -- the answer you have to kindly provide us with.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In those cases -- these cases are not adjudicated. There is not a final judgement. Only a certain stage in the proceedings was completed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Now, General, would you turn to paragraph 4, called "Basic problems." ," which is also on the page that's in front of you. And you talked about the difficulties of the work of the prosecutor of a large number of cases in a very short period of time. Sometimes the lack of legal evidence. And then you go on to say: "There's a slight increase in more complex crime, with an increasing number of perpetrators committing serious crimes, which represents a threat to society and requires greater engagement of the competent organs in order to uncover and prevent crimes." Is that something you noticed at the time?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And, again, though it might be repetitive, but I think it's important: What were the sources of your information? How did you -- this gradual -- this increase in crime, where did you get that from?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: This is all from the reports that I received from the courts and the prosecutor's offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And was this something that concerned you, this increase in crime and the lack of -- the ability to --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, every increase in the number of crimes, especially if we're talking about the complex and seriousness -- serious crimes, this is something that is of concern for -- for anyone dealing with this kind of issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And as a result of this concern, would you look at paragraph 6.3 of your report and tell us what that is. And that's on page 3D11-0407 in the English. Okay, and 6.3. Right. We might need -- no, I think that's fine. This -- this paragraph, General, says: "For units and organs at other levels." And it says: "All unit officers must immediately report to the competent military prosecutor any crimes and their perpetrators so that they can be prosecuted, and any officers who do not adhere to this will be made accountable and the strictest measures will be applied against them." Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And at about that time or slightly before that time, did you discuss your concerns about this, about the increasing number of crimes with General Matovic? And if you did, tell us what was that discussion and who General Matovic is.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, when I wrote this report, the first person that I acquainted with it was General Matovic, because he was my immediate superior. We analysed the situation and we made our assessments, and this was something that merited our attention, and we proposed the measures that had to be taken at the lower levels, not only preventative -- not only sanctions but preventive measures that would prevent other people from committing the same kind of acts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And did you follow through and draft an order to be signed by General Ojdanic on 10 May 1999, and that order reflected in tab 7 of 3D1110, which is 3D11-0320 in the English --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I just want to object to the leading nature of that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It would be better just to show him the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: That's fine. I have no problem with that. Yes. And by the way, this is also 3D483. It's already marked as a Defence exhibit. I think it's in evidence. But, again, we're following the tab structure, Your Honours. And if you would look at 3D11-0320 - that's in the English - and 3D11-0315 in the B/C/S. We'll wait for the B/C/S to come up. There it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Do you see that, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Just tell us what that is.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: This is an order that I prepared myself for the signature of the chief of the Supreme Command Staff, General Ojdanic. It was distributed to all the units. They all had to familiarise themselves with the contents of the order. And attachments were appended to this order, the excerpts from the Criminal Code of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. That dealt with the violations of the international humanitarian law. This order has a number of paragraphs. The first paragraph envisages that all the commanders at all levels in the units and all the superior commanders have to take all the necessary measures in their units to ensure that during combat and when not in combat all the unit members should abide by the provisions of the international law of war. So this is an imperative that had to be stressed once again. And it was brought to the attention of all the commanders of all the units that they are held personally responsible for any violations that they commit themselves or any violations committed by their subordinates. So the personal responsibility is stressed here. The commanders of all units and all the superior officers have to take all measures to prevent violations of laws and customs of international law of war if they knew about any violations yet failed to take measures to prevent them. And in paragraph 4, every officer should be held personally responsible if he knew that any such violations were committed and if he fails to take appropriate proceedings against such -- such perpetrators. And every person shall gather evidence against such persons and shall submit a criminal report. So this order was drafted in order to ensure that preventive measures are taken and also to sanction all violations of international humanitarian law, regardless of who the perpetrator is. This was distributed to commanders of all strategic groups and the task was to study that in the units and that all units should comply with it in their work.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I'm going to ask one more question on this, General. The -- in paragraph 6, there's -- there's an annex to the order which is mentioned, and it's -- it says that all -- all those reading the order should go through the annex regarding criminal liability for war crimes and other serious violations. And there was an annex attached to this report; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: May I inquire, Your Honour, I don't have an English translation of the annex, and I wonder if one exists. It doesn't appear to be in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes, I didn't have that until very recently. In 3D483, it's not attached. It's come -- yes, we will make an English translation available to Mr. Hannis right away.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And is there an annex attached? I'd be glad to show it to you, if it would help you. Do you want me to show you the annex?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And the annex, just very, very briefly, provides for war crimes against civilians and various other acts that -- that commanders should pay attention to and should warn their units about. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is the key issue, among other things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Gojovic, this -- this was prompted, you told us, by an increase in criminal conduct. What was the general nature of the increase in criminal conduct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, from the reports that I received from the courts, from the president of the supreme military court and from the supreme military prosecutor, if you monitor that, you become aware of the increase in the number of persons against whom criminal reports were filed, who were prosecuted and tried. You could see that several perpetrators would commit a certain crime. That was a trend. And this was something that required the attention on the part of the Supreme Command Staff; attention should be drawn to this to prevent any further increase in the level of crime, on the one hand; and on the other, to improve the efficiency of the -- in the work of the military courts and the organs that were involved in detecting the crimes in the field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What were the crimes which were being committed more regularly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in most cases, these were crimes against property. There were quite a few murders, multiple murders, and serious crimes of robbery with -- involving homicide. This was carried out by some renegade groups that were no longer under the control of their commands and then they perpetrated those crimes. And it was evident that this type of conduct was very dangerous. The conduct of such small group us that became loose cannons, that were out of control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I assume these are members of the VJ.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Now, following the war, did you write a report on the work of the military judicial organs during a state of war?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And I'm going to refer you to your report of September 6th, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And I would like to say at this point, for the record, Your Honour, there is an earlier report that we've marked as an exhibit of June 20, 1999. This report amplifies on that, gives more current data. I've spoken to Mr. Hannis about it. There's also an error in that earlier report. I've -- I've told Mr. Hannis about the error. He -- I don't know whether he's going to want to cross-examine on it or not, but I want to just make it clear for the record there is the earlier report. We're going to go to this report, 'cause I think it's -- it's more expansive and it's -- it's more accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Tell us about that report. It's -- by the way, it's 3D986. And it's at 3D06-0001 in B/C/S and 3D07-0375 in English. And, General, this is a report of September 6, 1999. And why did you write this report?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was completed at that time. Why was it written?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes. By the way -- yes. By the way, we might put up 3D07-0376. I think you've got the covering page in English. If you'd put up the next page in English, which is the first page of the report. That's it. Yes. Why -- how did you come to write this report?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, after the war ended and once all the data had been collated, the chief of the General Staff, General Ojdanic, through his operations organs ordered all sectors in the General Staff, all the organisational units in the General Staff, within their purview during the war, that they should submit a detailed report on their work, the problems, the difficulties they had encountered, in order to study that and to draw some lessons from it. This was the purpose of this report: To create a file, some documents that would be then used to study the work, the practice, and to see where the difficulties lay in terms of establishment, organisation, in order to eliminate those deficiencies in any further plans. That was the purpose of this report. It was to be filed and to be used at a later date to study the work of those organs during the war, what problems, what difficulties they encountered, and to draw conclusions how to improve the operation of those organs in the future. So that was the process of that -- purpose of that report. It is a voluminous report. It includes all the work from the time when the state of war was declared until the end of their operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: All right. And if we could turn to page 3D07-0382 in the English and 3D06-0006 in the B/C/S. Could you make it a little bit -- the top two paragraphs a little bit larger, please, top three paragraphs. And then the same with the B/C/S. Just the top -- yeah, that's fine. That's fine. Okay. Now, we have some numbers again. I don't know -- I hope it will clear this up, Your Honours, but let's -- let's just see. You have -- it says in your report that "Military prosecutors receive add total of" -- and again, this is as of September, correct, 19 -- 1999; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: It says: "Military prosecutors have received a total of 19.701 criminal reports, submitted requests for investigations of 5.630 persons and indicted 7.097 persons. Military courts completed 3.052 investigations and issued 3147 judgements. In addition, they carried out 280 on-site investigations," et cetera. And do you have those figures listed in your report at the end of your report? Have you compiled those figures in your report? And I'll specifically refer you to 3D-- in B/C/S 3D06-0014, in the B/C/S; and in the English 3D07-0390. Is it possible -- yeah, there we go. So, General, do you recognise that as an attachment to your report and does that set forth the figures you just testified to?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's for the September report. The figures are somewhat higher than the ones submitted in the 21st of June report. The simple reason is that it covers the period ending on the 25th of June. The state of war was ended on the 26th of June, so this covers this period. In the five or six days, the courts intensified their work and they tried to complete all the cases that were in the final stages. So this is why the -- we have this final figure. The report of the 21st, the data was compiled on the 18th and the 19th, so the figures are somewhat lower. You should not be confused by that, because this report -- the cut of date was the 20th [as interpreted] of June and this report in the September -- in September summarises all the data -- the cut of date was the 26th of June, because that's when the state of war ended. That is why there is a discrepancy in the figures, but that should not confuse you. But if you look at the number of adjudicated cases, there is precious little of those, so there is no major discrepancy there, but there is a big discrepancy in the number of criminal reports and the requests for investigation, because military prosecutors wanted to get as much done as possible in the period until the end of the state of war, which ended on the 26th of June. I don't know whether I was clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Your Honour, is it time for a break? Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Gojovic, we have to break at this stage for 20 minutes. Could you please leave the courtroom with the usher and we will see you again at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: General, we were talking about the number of criminal judgements that had been entered in -- in these cases, and I'd like to ask you: The great majority of these proceedings, of these criminal proceedings, were what -- for what crimes? The overwhelming majority were for what crimes?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the greatest part of them fell under Article 214 of the Criminal Code, that is, failure to respond to the mobilisation call-up; and Article 217, that is, going AWOL from one's unit. But in those circumstances of general mobilisation, many people did not respond to the call-up and proceedings were initiated against a great number of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And according to your report, General, this constituted some 88 per cent of the cases; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And what were the remaining 12 per cent?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: The remaining 12 per cent encompassed all other criminal acts committed at that time; that is, criminal acts against one's person, life or limb, and criminal acts against property. They were at the same time the criminal acts that were the best monitored.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: When you say "life or limb," what are the specifics we're talking about? What kind of crimes related to life and limb?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: All the criminal acts where the target, the victim is a human being; that is, all forms of murder, regardless of how they were perpetrated, all bodily arm -- harm or abuse, including rape. Those were the criminal acts encompassed by this general name, where the object of attack is a human being.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Were there war crimes included within this life-and-limb category?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: This category also encompasses war crimes, because they include murders.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: But you don't have any specifics in this report, do you, sir, on war crimes?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: In that report, they fall in the category of these criminal acts. There is no separate rubric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Now, General, simply what did you conclude in this report? What was your conclusion?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, my conclusion in that report was that the courts in those specific circumstances, within a relatively short space of time - that is, two, two and a half months - worked very efficiently, managing to deal with a great number of cases, a great number of cases were initiated and a high percentage of them were completed in those circumstances which were very difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And when you completed your report in September 1999, was General Ojdanic still the chief of the army's General Staff?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Did you discuss your report with him?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: No, not in September. It went to the operations department and the institute for war information, for purposes of study.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Now, General Ojdanic eventually became the Minister of Defence. Do you recall that? In February 2000.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And what was your job in February 2000?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: I was still at the General Staff. A bit later I moved to the legal department of the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And did you eventually compile a report dealing with war crimes and other serious crimes committed during the Kosovo war?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And when did you do that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: I made that report in September/October 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And why did you compile this report?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: A commission was established at that time, a commission of the Ministry of Defence for cooperation with the Tribunal in The Hague, because there had been some requests to submit certain documentation and information regarding proceedings underway here, so the ministry set up this commission in which I was deputy chairman, and I worked on that commission to gather this kind of data on criminal acts that have been perpetrated and can be qualified under the provisions of the international humanitarian law.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And is that report contained in tabs 18A and 18B of Defendant Exhibit 3D1110? You can just answer that "yes" or "no."

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And is that report, to your knowledge, also listed as a Prosecution Exhibit 955?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Probably. I am not up to snuff with the figures.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: You're not the person to ask that, but I'll just note, for the record, Your Honours, that it is 955. Now, upon what was this report based? Upon -- your -- your report of September 2001, upon what was it based?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: It was based on the report of the military court in Nis that had been submitted to the supreme military court, and I got it from there. So it was based on information provided by the military court in Nis, which had received all cases from military courts of The 3rd Army, that is, the military court of the -- the military district of Pristina, the command of the Nis Corps and the command of the Nis army. So all of these cases had been submitted to the military court in Nis for further processing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And is that information for the military court in Nis reflected in tab 17 of Defendant Exhibit 3D1110?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And that's also, Your Honours, Prosecutor's Exhibit 954. And for the record, tab 17 covers pages 3D11-0496-0562, and I should mention that tab 18 is divided into 18A and 18B. 18B is the crime of rape, 18A is all other crimes and is in the record at 3D11-- this is again Defendant Exhibit 3D110. 18A is 3D11-0645-0714. And 18B is 3D11-0728-0730.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So the short of it is, General, that tab 18 was based on tab 17; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Now, after you prepared this report, did you discuss it with General Ojdanic? And if you did discuss it, when did you discuss it and what was said?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I discussed it with him. While he was still Minister of Defence and while I was still chief of the legal department at the Ministry of Defence, he asked data on criminal acts processed at military courts during wartime to be organised, so that was finally done. I familiarised him with the situation, based on that data, and I discussed it with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Did you discuss the number and type of war crimes that you found and that you compiled in this report?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: I informed him of the numbers and information that I had gathered, and I showed him how it was shown in the report, how it was reflected. I tried to make it very obvious and easily understandable for anyone who is not a lawyer, and I thought it was easily understandable for him as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And what was his response to that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: His first reaction was that the report was very well done, very clear, and his only remark was that there were not many prosecutions and trials for these crimes except for crimes against property, because all robberies and similar crimes were included in the category of war crimes. It can easily be put under "war crimes," although they had initially been qualified differently. And there were also some crimes involving war crimes of murder, et cetera, were shown in the category of crimes against civilian population of the ethnic Albanian community. The discrepancy was considerable and we discussed why many of these perpetrators were not found and apprehended, so I provided him with some explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And are you saying that he said that -- he noted that there were not that many war crimes reflected in your report? Was that what he said? Or you -- if not, tell us what he did say.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he noticed that in the report, and he said that if you compare the figures of, for instance, how many victims and -- were -- were detected and processed without the perpetrators being detected he couldn't understand how come so many crimes were reported and how come that investigating bodies failed in all that time to identify the perpetrators and take action. I explained to him that in times of war, it's very difficult to identify perpetrators and find them, because the perpetrators hide very well. There is an atmosphere of fear, so that even those in the immediate surroundings of perpetrators are reluctant to report them. And even in cases when only fighting men were concerned, this seemed to be true as well. That is the flip side, the negative side of solidarity.
