But it is typical of all soldiers that they are bound by ties of solidarity regardless of the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And by unknown crimes -- in your report, had you noted a number of crimes that were committed where the perpetrators were not known but that investigations were being carried out? Is that true?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Now, General, do you know of a single reported war crime that was not investigated and processed through the criminal justice system?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: No, not a single one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Anything that we found out served as a basis for initiating proceedings by the competent military prosecutor and the military prosecutor took every step to shed light on the case and to gather as much information and facts as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And to make it clear, General, when I say "war crimes," I mean murders, multiple murders, rape, arsons, robbery, looting, the classic crimes of war. And given that definition, were all reported war crimes investigated and processed through the system; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Do you have any information whatever that General Ojdanic covered up or concealed the commission of any war crime?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: No. On the contrary, he constantly assisted that there shouldn't be any failure in that respect, that all perpetrators should be detected, and that every crime should be detected.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Every consequence of every crime as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Now, to summarise your report about war crimes committed against civilians and murders of civilians - and that's, again, in tab 18 and Prosecution Exhibit 955 - do you recall the total figures regarding the number of perpetrators and the number of victims?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: In that overview, we have totals for criminal acts that I evaluated, I believe objectively as war crime against civilian population, beginning with the classical war crime against civilian population, all forms of murder, all forms of multiple murder, all cases of robbery involving homicide. There was a total of 372 persons prosecuted. In crimes against life and limb, that is murders, perpetrators were prosecuted. There were in total 33 known perpetrators. Later on after the end of the war another four were prosecuted. That makes 37. And still later two more were found. In total, 39. As for victims of the crimes, there were 40 arising from these cases, and the victims were members of the ethnic Albanian community. In addition to that, there were some cases of rape that were detected and prosecuted; whereas, the second part deals with all forms of crime against property, such as large-scale thefts of property from the population, civilian ethnic Albanian population. Those were crimes against the civilian population. There were other crimes in which the injured party was an ethnic Albanian. In total, there were 601 victims in 11 localities, and in those cases, all judicial steps were taken by the judiciary; however, the results were not adequate because only a short amount of time was available and our units withdrew from Kosovo soon thereafter, so there was not much time for detecting perpetrators of those crimes. However, these cases are still ongoing and even now as we speak, the competent military prosecutor is still working on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Now, General, your report speaks for itself, but there are two or three matters in the report that I do think need clarification. I want to ask you about those now. I notice that there are a number of charters under Article 14, murder and multiple murder, and just a few charters under war crimes, as such, Article 142. Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: The article is 47.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes. What did I say?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: You said 14. That's Article 47 of the Criminal Code of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I misspoke. Article 47.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we have a much greater number of those crimes, and fewer of them were processed as war crime against civilian population under Article 142. Those were cases in which the superior officer ordered his subordinates to commit a crime. That was the classical form of war crime. In all other cases where there is no involvement of the superior officer in the commission of the crime, those murders were qualified by the competent prosecutors as multiple murders, and when there was one victim, it was qualified as murder, because the available sentence under the law of Serbia was much higher. The most severe sentence is the death sentence. And for the war crime, under Article 142 the lower sentence was five years and the highest, twenty years. So the prosecutors opted for the more severe sentence, which I believe is completely justified for the point of view of prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Another matter that I think needs clarification is that a number of these investigations were deferred to various district courts. For example, district court in Kraljevo or in Valjevo, that kind of thing. What's all that about if why were certain prosecutions deferred to district courts? Please tell the Trial Chamber about that.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: In all those cases where the perpetrator was a military person or a reserve soldier, after the state of war ended, the perpetrators were demobbed. They were no longer soldiers. For such cases, therefore, the military court was no longer qualified. When the perpetrator is no longer in service, the jurisdiction of the military court ceases and such cases are deferred to the district court. Usually the principal use is territorial, according to the locality of where the crime was perpetrated. If that was not possible, they were deferred to the court in the place of residence of the perpetrator and the proceedings went on under the same legislation that the military prosecution was guided by. The military courts continued to have jurisdiction only over those who remained in the army, and there were very few of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: All right. And then -- and another matter I think that should be clarified is that none of these crimes specifically list any sentences that were imposed. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: No, not at that time, because for such crimes, war crimes and multiple murder, there weren't any. And within the short time available, the -- the court in question did not manage to complete the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Have you since learned of certain sentences that were imposed in these cases?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: I did find out about certain cases. I found out either from courts directly or from the press. I believe around 11 cases were adjudicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And very -- very briefly tell us what you found out.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: I don't quite understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Tell us, if you remember - or I can direct you to the report, if you'd like - but do you remember the sentences that were applied to various individuals that you've now since learned about?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I learned that sentences from seven, eight, even fourteen years were meted out. I believe the maximum one was fourteen years imprisonment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Well, let's be specific. How about Dragisa Petrovic? Do you remember he was charged with murder? Do you remember what his sentence was?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I believe he got nine years.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And Nenad Stamenkovic and Tomica Jovic. Do you remember their sentences?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: I think they got a bit less. Four or five years perhaps, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Well, does seven years -- I know I'm leading here, but does seven years sound correct? If you don't remember, say so.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, all right, I don't remember, but seven years would be an appropriate sentence, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Forget about whether it would be an appropriate sentence. If your memory is four or five year, we're going to have to stick with that. All right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, this is at 3D11-0650 in the cases that I just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What I'm not understanding at all here, Mr. Sepenuk is the emphasis that was placed earlier on the importance of prosecuting in the most serious court because of the potential of the death penalty. And this evidence is that the longest sentence imposed for any crime during this whole conflict was 14 years. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I think that's true, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And by the way, on that subject, General, you've provided a brief distribution of crimes in your report, but do you know or not know what these individuals were eventually convicted of? Is that clear? Is my question clear? Do you know what --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it's clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: What was --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Eventually, wherever the case involved murder, they were convicted of war crime against civilian population, because the Defence assisted on that, so the courts re-qualified the case as one of war crime against civilian population, which is legally justified and completely appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Let me ask my question again. You have provided in the report a brief description of the crime; correct? It can be answered "yes" or"no."

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: But do you know when you're discussing sentences, seven year, five years, whatever, do you know in fact what any of these individuals were convicted for? Do you understand that question?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: I understand the question. Some were convicted of the charges that were leveled against them. In some cases, the charges of murder and war crime was dismissed and the charges of robbery or aggravated robbery remained and they were convicted of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Gojovic, are you saying it is the right of the accused person to choose whether he will be prosecuted for multiple murder or prosecuted for a war crime?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. This is the right of the prosecutor. The prosecutor issues an indictment, and he decides what's -- how to qualify in legal terms the criminal act. And then during the trial, depending on the evidence in the dossier, the court may re-qualify the act and the prosecutor may do so on the basis -- may request that this be done on the basis of the facts. The accused does not have the opportunity to do that. He is merely defending himself and trying to point out that the crime he committed was less severe than the one he is charged with. And it is up to the court to accept or not to accept certain legal qualification of the act, on the basis of all the evidence that was put in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does that mean, then, that when you completed this report, no one had been convicted for murder throughout the conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in the overview, I think there is something, but I don't think that any cases were finalised. But if it is not shown in the overview, that means that none of them were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And, again, just to complete the picture of actual sentences that have come to your knowledge, do you have knowledge of Dragoljub Cirkovic, his sentence?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I know that he was convicted, but I really can't tell you now off the top of my head what was the final sentence that was imposed on him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Do you have notes with you, General, on these cases?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I -- I do. I do have my notes here in the briefcase, but I'm not using them now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I had instructed the witnesses -- the witness, Your Honour, not to use notes at all, but I think we're in an area now where it might be permissible. At least, I would ask the Court's permission to just let him consult his notes on this. These are not official documents. These are simply notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, if he's going to be using them, Your Honour, I'd like to have a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: That's -- I have no problem with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there a copy?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: There's -- no, I don't think there's a copy. He's just got it noted on a piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, at the break, you would need to get and it copy it, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- to satisfy Mr. Hannis' request. Meanwhile, Mr. Gojovic, you may refer to your notes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I found it. Dragoljub Cirkovic, he was convicted and sentenced to eight years in prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And if you wouldn't mind going back to the one you were not certain about before, that's Nenad Stamenkovic and Tomica Jovic. Do your notes reflect the sentences they received?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Nenad Stamenkovic, Tomica Jovic -- Dragisa Petrovic, he was sentenced to nine years. Nenad Stamenkovic was sentenced to seven years. And Tomica Jovic also to seven years. They previously received milder sentences, but the prosecutor appealed and the Court increased the sentences.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What were the crimes for which these seven-year sentences were imposed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were first charged with the murder of several persons, but then it was re-qualified as a crime against civilian population under Article 142, and that was the crime that they were convicted of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But do you know what they actually did? What physical act they were actually convicted of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can read it here. Dragisa Petrovic, in the area or village of Susice, where his unit was deployed. Ordered Nenad Stamenkovic and Tomica Jovic to kill Rukija and Feriz Krasniqi, an elderly pair who didn't leave the village, and they did so by discharging their automatic rifles at them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And that's what you get seven years for in that system of justice, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dragisa Petrovic was sentenced to nine years, and the actual perpetrators, they got seven years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, just to clarify, maybe it doesn't need clarification, but I take the thrust of your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: That was -- you read from a brief description of the crime. Correct, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: But you know in fact what these men were sentenced for. I mean, you weren't at the trial. You didn't attend the trial. You don't know really the facts as adjudicated. Do you or do you not?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't, but this is the essence: Two persons were killed, two elderly civilians were killed during the war. So this is a war crime against the civilian population, and that's what they were convicted of.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And I think the last -- not quite the last. But how about Nebojsa Stankovic? That was an attempt to kill one person. And it's at 3D11-0656 of 3D1110.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: What was that sentence?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Four years in prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. And finally, General, as I understand it, that there is a series of cases that you very recently learned about and, in fact, just discussed with me yesterday. And would you just summarise very briefly those cases. I'm talking about the cases involving Mancic, Radojevic, Tesic, and Sergej.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Sergej Misel, yes. Those were four persons who were indicted at a later stage. That was in 2002. They were convicted. The final sentences they received -- Mancic received 14 years in prison. Radojevic was sentenced to nine, Tesic to seven, and Sergej Misel to five years in prison. Upon the review of the Supreme Court of Serbia, sitting in a special chamber, this conviction was quashed and we now have a retrial. This was done for procedural reasons. There were some procedural deficiencies in the previous trial and the Supreme Court quashed this conviction and the case was -- went up for retrial.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And just for the sake of accuracy, I take it these were cases, as I understand it, where the charges against all the four were all the same, and that is with killing two Albanians -- two persons of Albanian nationality. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And just, again, to clarify it, the initial sentences, as I understand it, were seven years for Mancic, five years for Radojevic, four years for Tesic, and three years for Misel, and those sentences were doubled by the appeals court; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: But then the court --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, almost doubled. For the first accused, yes. But for the other accused, it was slightly less than double. But, yeah, you could say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And the Supreme Court of Serbia reversed the judgement because of newly discovered evidence. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the Supreme Court of Serbia quashed. It did not reverse it. The case went for retrial.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, General?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: That's all I have, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Cepic?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, good morning --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Just a minute. I hope you forgive me for that. General, you have kindly spoken of 2.393 cases which you observed were closed in your reports. Have you been able to scrutinise the record of any of these cases for ascertaining whether the closure was in accordance with law and principles of justice, or you just accepted the figuration as it came to you and reported it accordingly? Was there a scrutiny of record - that's my question - of those cases? I'm very grateful.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I didn't go through the cases. This would be a huge task. That was not my job. On the basis of the information that I received in the reports from the supreme military court and the supreme military prosecutor's office who had obtained the data, I merely statistically processed the data and showed it in the overview. The cases that are shown at tab 18, this thing that we were just discussing, I went to the military court in Nis for the majority of those cases, and that's where I was able to look into most of those cases just to see what the status of the record is. But it was objectively impossible to go through the thousands of those cases, 2.000 cases. That was not the purpose of the report, to get into the merits of the case but just to get a statistical overview of the work-load of those courts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: So there was no scrutiny and not even a few cases were picked up for purposes of acquaintance with the record and what had happened with the procedure. Forgive me if I said so. Does that mean that you were forwarding figures in a mechanical way and reflecting these in your report without giving any views on the quality of things? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I took the data that I got at their face value, and there was no reason for me to doubt the accuracy of the data. There may be some kind of a statistical error, but that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm going to violate a cardinal rule now. I'm going to ask a question that I don't know the answer to. And I'm blaming my brethren who are experts in the continental law system, who talked to me at the break. This may make things more confusing or, on the other hand, it may clarify. Further examination by Mr. Sepenuk:

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, when an investigative judge refers a case to the prosecutor -- and by the way, let me back up a little bit. In your system, you have investigative judges, do you not?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And when the investigating judge refers the case to the prosecutor, does that constitute a closing of the case as far as the investigating judge is concerned?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He did his job. He closes his case. And he in any reports states that this case is closed, that the investigation is completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So whatever elucidation that has, Your Honours, I mention it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sepenuk, this was in tab 15, I think. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: This gets back to the question that Your Honours was asking before. I'm not sure we have that problem with the -- I mean, really I'm sure the figures that you want to look at are in that September report and this report. I don't think the report that, Judge Chowhan you were asking the questions on had the accuracy of these later two reports. But to the extent that it was troubling, Your Honour, that might be one way of looking at it, I must say I'm not familiar with the continental system. So, again, a couple of my brethren grabbed me and said, "This is the situation."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Further cross-examination by Mr. Cepic:

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, I said good morning but I failed to introduce myself. Let me do that now. My name is Djuro Cepic and I'm representing General Lazarevic. [In English] Please Exhibit Number 2490, P2490.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, my learned colleague Mr. Sepenuk asked you about the work of the investigating judge, and I would now like to ask you some more questions, but could you please first look at the part of the statement that will be shown in front of you on the screen very carefully. [In English] Could we have paragraphs 17 and 18, please. [Interpretation] While we're waiting for this to come up, General, we have a statement by Dr. Gordana Tomasevic. She's a forensic medicine specialist. She testified in this case as a Prosecution witness. General, could you please look at paragraph 17 and 18, where it is stated that General Pavkovic then verbally ordered Dr. Tomasevic to go to Stari Cikovo [phoen]. She said that she had asked for a court order and that there was no court order. And then later on in paragraph 18, she states that in addition to the military crime technicians, that an on-site investigation was carried out by military crime technicians and bodies were discovered in situ. There where they had been set on fire. Were you able to look at this, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: My general -- my question to you, General, is whether in this particular case, whether everybody concerned acted accordance with the law.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I can see, this is an on-site investigation. The crime scene technicians were there. They performed the investigation and the photo file and the doctor, as the forensic medicine specialist, visually inspected the bodies and ascertained that the bodies were carbonised. Procedurally speaking, this is done properly in investigation terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Let us just make this clear. Is this in line with the provisions on the Law on Criminal Procedure?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is in accordance with the Law on Criminal Procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So no order from the investigating judge was needed. The crime scene technicians could have done that on their own.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: This was an urgent -- urgent measures needed to be taken and there was no need for any order on the part of the investigating judge. She's talking about a fee, but this is absurd because she was sent there on behalf of the military medical academy. She is there in an official capacity. She is not there in her private capacity. She was not required to give her opinion as an expert in a private capacity.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. [Previous translation continues] ... [In English] Exhibit Number 3D1110, tab 15. 15, tab 15. Could we -- I think that will be much more easy if we have Exhibit number P2826. My learned friend Mr. Hannis has underlined that that is the same document. Could we have paragraph number 2.3, please. [Interpretation] General, in paragraph 2.3, - the heading is "The 3rd Army - my learned colleague Mr. Sepenuk asked you a couple of questions about that, but let me go back to that because I need some clarifications. In the third passage of this paragraph, the third passage that begins with the words "military judicial organs attached to the Pristina Corps Command have encountered in their work." And then it says: "Terrorism, murder, robbery, theft." That's in brackets. My question to you is: Do you know that the military judicial organs had jurisdiction over the crimes of terrorism committed against the personnel of the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they had that kind of jurisdiction. That's what I said a little while ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And was there a substantial number of such acts, terrorist acts targeting the personnel?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, those terrorist groups mostly targeted the Army of Yugoslavia, the MUP organs, and the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Those terrorist acts, did they target civilians regardless of their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I take it that your questions, Mr. Cepic, relate to a particular period of time? And if so, can we have clarification? Because the report is dealing with the situation after the 16th of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could I spread my question for the longer time period?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it's useless to us, that sort of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is all about the operation of the military judicial organs, and there is no point in using a witness like this to go into vague general statements about KLA terrorism, which we all know was happening on a fairly widespread basis throughout the area. I assume when you're asking questions of this witness, you'll be talking about the period after the 16th of April, when he took up his post, unless you're going to establish another foundation for him to give evidence about a different period in time. So please try to focus the questions in a way that will -- will assist us.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You heard His Honour, Judge Bonomy. Let me rephrase the question, then. Mr. Gojovic, are you aware that in this period that was indicated by His Honour that the terrorists -- that several thousands of Army of Yugoslavia personnel were killed in those terrorist acts and that they -- those acts were prosecuted?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: I do know that a large number of army personnel got killed in terrorist acts, but I did not have this kind of information. I didn't know about any prosecutions that were brought against members of those terrorist groups. This could be done only if they were accessible to the law enforcement. But I did not have that kind of data.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. You explained to us about the murders and the sentences envisaged for that kind of act. Now we are going to be dealing with robbery in accordance with the provisions of the Republic of Serbia Criminal Code, in Articles 168 and 169, robbery was dealt with, aggravated robbery and robbery. Could you please tell us, what was the special maximum sentence for the crime of aggravated robbery, as described in Article 169?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: I explained a little while ago. Aggravated robbery contains murder, subsumes murder in itself, and the same kind of sentences envisaged for those crimes as for multiple murder; from ten years --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the maximum sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the maximum there, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, could you please tell us what was the maximum sentence.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: It was the death penalty and the lower sentence was ten years.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: If there are any mitigating circumstances, can the sentence then go below the minimum?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: No, not when these crimes are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are there in your report any examples of a sentence in excess of ten years being imposed for robbery?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this overview, at tab 18, there is a certain number of people who were sentenced or convicted of aggravated robbery. And as for the sentences, I can have a look, if you're interested. I think that this is Majovic and I think another group of them. There were ten or eleven of them. It's in this overview. Let me just have a look. There are seven of them: Aggravated robbery and robbery, but I can't see whether the case was adjudicated or not, but seven of them were indicted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just to clarify one point. It's a minor point, but I still feel we ought to clarify it. In the meantime, in our country the death penalty has been abolished, has it not?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: The latest amendments to the Criminal Code of Serbia, in compliance with European standards, abolished the death sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: In view of this, in our legal system is the system of the milder law applicable?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I believe this happens in every country. It is always the law that is most favourable to the accused that is applied. If the new law is more favourable for the accused, that's the one that's applied; if it's the old law, then that's the one that's applied. So it's always in favour of the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, now a procedural question. When does the obligation of a commanding officer who reports a crime end?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: A military commander is duty-bound if a crime is committed to take all steps to preserve the traces and discover the perpetrator. When he informs the prosecutor or a criminal report is submitted or the military police and military security are alerted, he has fulfilled his duty. From that point on, it's the organs of detection that the competent prosecutor is in charge of, that take over. So any legal responsibility and the legal obligation of the commander then stops.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Can he influence the work of the courts, of the prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: No. These organs are fully independent in their decision-making and assessments of the cases that have been reported to them, a criminal report filed and criminal proceedings instituted.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ivetic, do you have anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Gojovic, you'll now be cross-examined by the Prosecutor. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned at the start of your evidence that before you were appointed general, Ojdanic came to see you and told you that he was trying to find someone to improve the operations of the military courts. What did he tell you about the nature and extent of the problems with the military courts at that time, as of the middle of April 1999? Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He told me briefly that there were certain difficulties in the organisation of the courts and their efficiency in the proceedings. This had been noticed. It had been observed. And there was a request that these difficulties be removed and that all the conditions for the most efficient possible functioning of the courts be established. I am referring both to the prosecutors and the courts and the technical services, the military detention units. It's a complex mechanism, just as the Tribunal here is a complex mechanism.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Did he describe the problems as being in part due to the personnel that were presently engaged in the process?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was the central issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did he indicate to you that there were also problems in matters being reported and investigated?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, no, because the submitting of reports is outside the judicial system. It's the commanding officers or the organs of the military police that file those. They are not part of the judiciary, so that was not what was at issue. It was rather the judicial proceedings themselves where the difficulties were observed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Mr. Sepenuk asked you about the -- the rules of conduct, the rules of conduct which you told us were printed on laminated cards, and you said at page 8, line 20 today that every single soldier had a copy. How do you know that, General? You didn't actually carry out a personal inspection of every soldier in the VJ to make sure he had a copy, did you?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not carry out an inspection, because that was not my job. It's the military inspectors that have to do that. But it was part of the equipment of every soldier. When I mobilised the military court, I had a file with the equipment given to every individual, and it included that plasticised card. So it's a set that is given to every soldier, just as every soldier is issued with weapons and so on, he's also issued with those laminated cards. It's part of his kit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I understand you'd be saying that's -- that's what was supposed to happen, and I understand that that's your belief, but as I recall, I believe -- I believe we've had some evidence in this case from -- from soldiers who served in the VJ who told us they did not have that card and that they had not been briefed about those laws and rules of conduct. So you don't know whether that's true or not, do you? There may have been a shortage of cards, for example.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: There were sufficient copies, but a soldier might have felt he didn't need it. He might have lost it or thrown it away. But when he puts on his boots, when he's given his equipment, his tent canvas and all that, it's part of his kit. Then he's given that as well. It's just simply a part of his kit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned the handbook for VJ in combat -- engaged in combat versus terrorism. You mentioned this handbook was distributed, I think, only to those soldiers engaged in those kind of operations. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it was intended for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And would -- under the circumstances, do you know if that would have been given to all soldiers in Kosovo in April 1999? How was that decided?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: That's not how I understood it and what I said. The handbook where terrorist actions are mentioned refers to the period outside of war. In 1990, there was a state of war, and then the rules of war were in force. But early in 1998 and earlier, when measures against terrorist groups were being undertaken, that's when those booklets were handed to those soldiers participating in anti-terrorist activities. But the one we are referring to was issued when there was no state of war, and then there was a different situation when there was a state of war, because then it was not only terrorist groups but the forces of the NATO pact which were conducting an aggression against Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: For the sake of clarity, 72, 4, it says 1999 and the witness says -- it says "1990" and it was 1999, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, had you finished your answer? Before I go to my next question.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. You --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I just back up a little and -- and clarify one thing. When you took over at the General Staff, who did you replace?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Before that, there was General Svetislav Ristic. He was the chief of the legal administration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And we see there right up until the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What became of him then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was relieved of that duty, and I think he retired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We were talking about -- well, you were talking with Mr. Sepenuk about the -- the criminal laws regarding murder and war crimes. You told us Article 142 had a sentencing range of five to twenty years? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And Article 47, murder, the sentencing range was from ten years to -- to the death penalty; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And multiple murder, is that the same sentencing range?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And what about voluntary manslaughter?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: That was a far milder sentence, up to five years.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And involuntary manslaughter?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, if it's involuntary, if it's an accident, then it's not a crime. If there is an intention, if it's premeditated -- if there's no intention, then it's negligence. But those are different legal qualifications, depending on the actual facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I -- I ask the question because in one of the -- one of the tables that I have- I think it's actually your Exhibit 955 - there are listed a number of cases involving "involuntary manslaughter," is how it's translated into English, Article 49. And I see one of those accused got a sentence of two years; another one got a sentence of one year and three months. So is it a criminal offence or not?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, those are all criminal offences, but probably it was done out of negligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. But for a violation --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: It was involuntary manslaughter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: For violation of Article 49, what is the sentencing range?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Those are aggravated cases of robbery. Let me just check. Well, there's paragraph 1 and paragraph 2. Paragraph 1 covers the use of force and weapons to take something from someone by force. That's aggravated robbery. In paragraph 2, if someone is deprived of his life, then that's aggravated robbery and the sentencing range is from ten years to the death sentence. So there are two paragraphs in that article. If threats and weapons were used only to take away things, that's one. And, two, if in doing that the other person was murdered, that's a more serious form. That's an aggravated form, and then the minimum sentence is ten years. There was such cases. We had several persons accused of that criminal offence in the period we are now talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, General, perhaps we're missing something in translation. I wasn't asking you about aggravated robbery. I was asking you about various degrees of homicide. You told me in Article 47 about the range for murder and for multiple murder. I ask you about voluntary manslaughter, which I understand is Article 48, and you told me the maximum sentence is up to five years. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And Article 49, which is translated into English as "involuntary manslaughter," what's the maximum sentence for that? If you know.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: For involuntary manslaughter, it's at -- five years max, but for voluntary manslaughter, it's not limited. But I have to look these things up, because I've never been able to memorise them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. You're not saying that the maximum penalty for voluntary manslaughter could also be the death penalty, are you?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. No, it's far less. I don't think it's more than ten years. It's not more than ten years.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you mentioned the death penalty was abolished or revoked in the Republic of Serbia in what year?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: The latest amendments, I think, were made in 2005 or 2004. There was a lengthy discussion about those amendments. I think it was actually in 2003 that the death penalty was abolished.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And how about in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia? Wasn't the death penalty abolished in 1993?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: It was abolished in the time of the SFRY, in 1990. And then the law was taken over by the FRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So in 1999, the death penalty was not a legal sentence in the Federal Republic; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: It was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, near the end of your testimony - I think in your discussion with Mr. Cepic, perhaps - you talked about the legal -- the legal concept of the lesser penalty applying, that an accused is entitled to receive a lesser penalty. How would that work, where in the Federal Republic there is no death penalty and in Serbia there was? Would it -- could a person still be sentenced to the death penalty even though the higher-level government, the republic, did not allow for it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: It's possible. It's possible, because according to the federal law, there is no death penalty and the person is tried for a certain crime. As for murder as envisaged in the republican law, that is not a criminal offence. That is legislated for at the federal level. I think I've been clear. The federal law provides for certain criminal offences, and there is no death penalty provided for those, so it would not apply if a person was being tried for a crime that is provided for in the federal law.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how would the military courts deal with the situation where there -- say I'm a defence attorney in the military court. I have a client charged with Article 47, death penalty eligible murder. Could I ask to the court, "no, I want my client charged under the federal provision for murder." Could he do that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: In the proceedings, in the way before that court, it's possible to proffer evidence and insist if the crime was perpetrated in wartime, then it might be a war crime against the civilian population rather than murder as such. And all defence counsel always adduced evidence to that effect, and then the courts would re-qualify the crime because all the circumstances indicated that this should be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, my understanding of this, if it helps - and it may be wrong - is that murder or multiple murder is not a crime under the federal court.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think you're right, Your Honour. I think that's what I understood the situation to be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But, General, in Kosovo in 1999 during -- during the conflict with NATO, in every instance where somebody from the VJ murdered a civilian, all those crimes would be eligible to be treated as war crimes against civilians under Article 142; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The -- am I correct that the only situation where a soldier in Kosovo in 1999 could have been charged with a death penalty murder and not entitled to have a -- have it treated as a war crime would be where he killed another VJ soldier, for example, or perhaps a MUP policeman,'cause they're not civilians? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So no death penalties were imposed for any murders in Kosovo in 1999; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. In the FRY, for the last 30 years not a single death penalty has been carried out, although such crimes have been committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And that means in the Republic of Serbia as well no death penalties carried out; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Is there any reason that a -- a VJ soldier who killed a civilian in Kosovo in 1999, assuming the appropriate mental state, is there any reason he could not be charged with both a violation of Article 142 and a violation of Article 47?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: He could not be charged simultaneously with two crimes for a single action if the consequences of the action amount to a death. So it can be only one criminal offence he's charged with. Whether it's murder under the republican law or Article 142, but kit not be both simultaneously for the same action.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I assume that applies to an aggravated robbery in which a death occurred. So he -- he couldn't be charged with aggravated robbery and murder. It would have to be one or the other. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, because it's subsumed in the criminal offence. Anyone who deprives someone of his life using weapons in order to deprive them of their property. It's a cumulative action.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you know -- do you know how prosecutors made the choice between charging someone in a particular killing with a violation of Article 142, Article 47, or the aggravated robbery statute? Because it seems to me that on many -- in many factual circumstances, any one of those three charges might apply.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Not in all cases. With aggravated robbery, that's a specific criminal offence. One takes away property and deprives someone of their life in order to do that. So that's one criminal offence. When we're dealing with murder or war crimes against civilians, the consequence is the same, the killing of a person, and then the prosecutor can decide how he's going to qualify the act and the prosecutor usually went for the more serious one, for the one with the higher sentence in order to have more room for manoeuvre and if the state of the evidence so indicated, he could then go for the lesser sentence, but he could not do that at a later stage. That's why -- he couldn't go for the higher -- higher sentence at a later stage, which is why they went for it at the outset, because then they would have more room for manoeuvre. He would have more room than if the lighter sentence were applied.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I -- can you explain for us a little bit about what you mean by "room for manoeuvre" in this context.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let's take a hypothetical situation. A soldier abandons his unit, runs away, goes off in the opposite direction. He bursts into a house or a coffee-shop and he kills ten people. If the prosecutor were to qualify this as a war crime, saying that in a time of war a multiple murder was committed, such a high sentence cannot be imposed. And then later on it's established that it was not a war crime but that it was a multiple murder carrying a far higher sentence but the prosecutor can no longer re-qualify -- he cannot amendment the indictment now, because from the outset he decided on the crime for which a lighter sentence is imposed. If, however, at the outset he went for multiple murder and then it's established that there was some kind of military assignment involved and that he can go for Article 142, some sort of mission, then he can do that at a later stage. I don't know if I've been clear enough now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I ask something, Mr. Gojovic, to try to clarify one aspect that's concerning the Judges. In the FRY, was any part of the territory, federal territory so that it did not strictly fall within either the Republic of Serbia or the Republic of Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No. The territory was integral and unified, and on the entire sovereign territory the law of the Federal Republic applied for designated criminal acts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: And so if a crime took place within the capital, what would be the choice? Which republican law will be applicable in that territory of the capital? There would be a capital territory. And if somebody commits a crime, now, here is somebody to decide whether it will be one republic or the other. How can that happen? And did -- did not your Penal Code have any prescription for -- for punishment against murder? That also. I mean, that's causing a bit of confusion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Criminal Code of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia did not envisage the criminal act of murder. That was regulated by republican laws. The federal law only deals with criminal acts against the federal state, the army, and some other institutions as covered by international conventions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: What about the capital territory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Every law applies on the entirety of the territory. So the federal law applies to the whole territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, regardless of where the crime was committed, and it is enforced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I'm not asking -- General, I interrupt you. I'm sorry. What I mean is if a crime takes place, let's say in the capital, let's say in the parliament building. Then what law would be applicable? Which -- of which of the republics? I mean, that is ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case -- well, the federal law applies wherever the crime envisaged is committed, be it in Belgrade, Nis, or whatever village. If the criminal act concerned is covered by the federal law. If the crime is covered by the republican law, then the law of Serbia applies to crimes committed in the territory of Serbia and the law of Montenegro applies to crimes committed in Montenegro. That is the principle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: If the crime takes place in the parliament building in the capital and which law -- and a murder takes place, which law will be applicable?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of the Republic of Serbia, if it's murder.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, is this an appropriate time for the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It would be. Thank you. Mr. Gojovic, we have to take another break at this stage for half an hour. If you could again go with the usher, please. We will resume at ten minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When we resume, we shall sit without Judge Chowhan, who has urgent personal reasons for not being here at the next session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, Mr. Sepenuk asked you about the report you prepared and later discussed with General Ojdanic. I think we're talking about Exhibit P955, which is tab 18 for you. You mentioned that there were a total of 372 persons prosecuted and in crimes against life and limb, that is, murders, perpetrators were prosecuted, there were in total 33 known perpetrators. And later on in the war, another four were prosecuted. That makes 37. And still later two more were found, for a total of 39. So is 39 the total number of VJ soldiers who were prosecuted for crimes against life and limb during the conflict between 24 March and -- and late June 1999? Is that the grand total?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what was -- if you know, what was the highest sentence, the highest number of years imposed for any one of those convicted for those crimes? Do you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. 14 years imprisonment, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, at page 50 today, line 13, you were speaking about Article 47. You mentioned that you had a greater number of those crimes and fewer were processed as war crimes against civilians. You said those were cases in which the superior officer ordered his subordinates to commit a crime. That was the classical form of war crime. So in those cases where a lower-ranking soldier, say a private, was ordered by a commander to -- to shoot civilians, in those cases the privates were prosecuted under Article 142 for -- for a war crime? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And is that -- is that because it was deemed to be more fair to prosecute them with the -- with the charge that carried a less-severe penalty because in essence they were carrying out an order from their superior? Is that why that was done?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: That was the appropriate legal provision. That was the textbook example of that criminal act. That's how it was described in the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in those -- in a factual scenario like that, what would -- what would the superior officer be charged with?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Also the same charge, under Article 142.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I -- I saw a description of -- of a -- a charge in a factual scenario like that where the officer was charged with inciting a war crime. Is that the proper terminology?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there is such a charge, incitement, ordering someone else to commit a criminal act is incitement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And is there any difference in the penalty for inciting, as opposed to the -- the principal act of murder? Or does it carry the same penalty?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: It carries the same penalty, although it's possible to punish responsibility for incitement harsher than perpetration. It depends on the criminal base and how the criminal responsibility is evaluated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in that factual scenario, say where we have a -- a major telling two privates to shoot civilians, they're charged with a war crime against civilians. Could he be charged with incitement to murder in that factual scenario?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: No, he can be charged with only one of them. Either Article 142, which seems to be obvious -- but privates cannot be charged with war crime against civilian population, and the one who ordered it cannot be charged with murder at the same time; incitement to murder, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. But if the -- if the privates had been charged with murder under Article 47, then the major, in my factual scenario, could have been charged with incitement to murder; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if, as I understood you to explain before, the prosecutor who wants more room to manoeuvre, in our factual scenario he could have charged the privates with murder and the major with incitement to murder, and then he would have had lots of room to manoeuvre in that case; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: He would have more room to manoeuvre insofar as he would be able to re-qualify it as a war crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: One of the things you are recorded on the English transcript as saying is that privates cannot be charged with a war crime against the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But then he goes on to say and the one who order it cannot be charged with murder at the same time. I think if you read it together, it -- it makes sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't -- it doesn't make sense to me, Mr. Hannis. I've tried.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's Correction: If I may, the sentence would read properly if it read "the privates cannot be charged with murder while -- or sorry, with war crime while the one who incited them is charged with murder."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I can ask another question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, that makes sense now. But if you want to pursue it, yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If I understood, General, then it seems like what you're saying is that -- that in that fact scenario those three individuals have to be treated separatory. So either they're charged as a murder or all charged with a war crime, with the major charged with inciting it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. But in your system -- because in my system, it could be done this way -- could there be some kind of later adjustment of the crime? Say they'd all been charged with the murder and the major charged with incitement to murder. If the prosecutor felt in fairness it would be appropriate to treat the privates more leniently and re-qualify their crime as a war crime against civilians, could the incitement to murder charge remain in place for the major, or would it have to be changed too? Do you follow?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: That, too, would have to be re-qualified into war crime against civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Or incitement to war crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I think I understand now. Thank you. Now, you mentioned that in the cases where the perpetrator was a military person, a reserve soldier, and after the state of war ended if he was demobilised, then the military court no longer had jurisdiction and the case had to be transferred to a civilian court. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And that's true no matter what stage the proceedings might be at with regard to the reserve soldier.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: It doesn't matter at what stage, except if the indictment has been confirmed by the relevant court, then the court continues with the case. Until that time, the case can be deferred to a civilian court. Since we had no exceptions of that kind, all such cases were deferred to civilian courts and they proceeded there, except in those cases when the accused continued to serve in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So if the indictment had been confirmed before the reserve soldier is demobilised, then the case could continue in the military court, even though that guy's not in the army anymore.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do I understand your answer to be you didn't have any such situations at the end of this war. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: We did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And explain for me briefly, if you could, how does the indictment get confirmed? By whom? And how long does that normally take?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: After the indictment is brought and the court receives it, the president of the trial chamber, which is going to deal with the case makes the indictment available to the accused and his Defence counsel. If they file an objection to the indictment, a Chamber decides on that objection, it can be granted, saying that there are deficiencies and shortcomings in the indictment and it has to be revised, and then the investigating judge goes on collecting new evidence. If the trial chamber rejects the objection, the indictment is thereby confirmed. If there have been no objections and all deadlines - namely, eight days from the issuing of the indictment - are expired, the indictment automatically become -- enters into force unless the president of the trial chamber himself finds that the indictment is imperfect and he returns it for further work. Once the indictment is confirmed, a trial date can be set and proceedings can start. The deadlines are rather short and that leaves more time for -- for actual work.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And let me back up, then, on -- on the front end of the process. Who presents -- who delivers the indictment to the judge?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Oh, I see Mr. Zecevic on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm so sorry. I believe the part of the answer by the witness has not entered the transcript. Actually witness says that this process takes rather a long period of time. And it wasn't recorded. I mean, maybe my friend can-- can deal with that once again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where do you say that should be in the answer, Mr. Zecevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The deadlines -- it's 88, 6: The deadlines are -- are short in fact, but the process takes a relatively long time to -- to reach this stage of the process, or something along these lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, let me approach it this way. And I know I'm asking you to make some rough estimates, but because of your experience, maybe you can help us. In this scenario in Kosovo, say a report was made of -- of war crimes against a civilian. And it's not a complicated case. You may have three perpetrators and two of them have -- have confessed. There's physical evidence on the scene. Photographs have been taken, et cetera. It's a relatively non-complex, straightforward case. Can you give us an estimate of how long it would take for that case, during the wartime conditions, which we understand made it more difficult -- would that be a matter of days or weeks or month to get to the stage where an indictment could be confirmed by a judge?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: There have been no cases, although objectively speaking if everything is so easily available and handy, the investigation condition completed, the necessary forensic procedures can be completed, and the indictment can be issued within two or three months. It can be done. But all these cases were complex and there were no such easy situations in which indictments could be raised while the state of war was still in force. Courts began to receive cases only in the second half of April. So it was a relatively short time. From these overviews, you can see how many cases were processed. In terms of statistics, that indicates a rather high degree of efficiency; although, courts, of course, first dealt with those cases that were easier and where the facts were clear. We did not have cases of the kind that you describe, where everything was documented and that could have been dealt with while the state of war was still in force, but we had no such clear-cut cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Do I understand you correctly that were there no cases involving life and limb in which indictments were confirmed before the end of the conflict in June 1999, or did -- did some cases manage to get processed before the end of the war, cases involving life and limb?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, there were some minor cases that included elements of war crime against civilian population. But in none of those cases did it come to the stage of valid indictment; otherwise, they would have been resolved, since it wasn't done within the state of war situation, that means that no indictments entered into force in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. For those reserve soldiers, at the end of the war how did they get demobilised? As soon as the -- as soon as the agreement is signed, are they automatically demobilised? Do they get an order? Does it take some time afterwards before they receive their paperwork? How did that work?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, after the state of war ceased, all the units were pulled out of Kosovo and demobilisation was affected within a relatively short time, not more than five or ten days.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And then the case that had previously been proceeding in the military court which is no longer viable once that reserve soldier is demobilised, to what -- to what civilian court does the military court defer? I understand the first option would be at the location where the crime occurred, but I guess as a practical matter, when we're talking about Kosovo in June 1999, that didn't happen. The cases would then be transferred to what civilian court? One in Serbia proper? Not Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: I understood the question. With a cessation of the state of war, under the law military courts and military prosecutor's offices must cease their work. They can no longer act in such cases. They were duty-bound to submit all their cases to the military court in Nis. So all the cases from Kosovo had to be placed before the military court in Nis. The military court in Nis took over all those cases and started to act upon them. And in those cases where the perpetrator was no longer in army service, the case would be deferred to the district court, but those cases from district courts from Kosovo and Metohija were relocated to Serbia proper. So it was to district courts in Serbia would deal with them if they had been constituted and had started working by that time. If not, they would be -- the cases would be forwarded to another court under the decision of the Supreme Court of Serbia, because that had been requested, and the relocation would be to a court which had jurisdiction in the place of residence of the perpetrator. So first -- the first priority, the first step would be the district court from Kosovo relocated to Serbia or to the place of residence of the perpetrator. In all those cases where a war crime is involved, nowadays they are tried before the special chamber for war crimes, unless a trial had started already.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when was that special chamber created?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: That was established ... Well, I didn't keep track, but I think it was in 2003 or 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Between 1999 -- the -- after the end of the war and the creation of that special chamber, then for a reservist who was demobilised, his case that previously had been pending in the military court would have been sent to a district court either in Kosovo or in his place of residence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, with a proviso that all courts in Kosovo and Metohija were relocated. They did not remain in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. They no longer functioned there. They were relocated to some other place, in Serbia. And that's where they received those cases for trial. For instance, the district court of Pristina was relocated and its base is now in Nis. Other courts were relocated to other places.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now -- now I understand. The court that previously had been -- the district court that previously had been in Pristina after the war for these purposes was relocated to Nis and the reservist who had been demobilised will either be tried there, if his crime happened in Pristina, or he could be tried in the district court in his place of residence. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who decided whether he would be tried in Nis for that Pristina crime or in his district court at his place of residence? How were those decisions made?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that is regulated by the Law on Criminal Procedure. If the local competent court is unable to deal with it- for instance, the district court of Prizren - it is the Supreme Court of Serbia which decides to which court it will then be delegated. There is no self-initiative or -- or liberal decision-making. There is a specific procedure which governs this issue. It's the so-called delegated local jurisdiction, territorial jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And does the defendant -- or does the accused have no right to request that Pristina court sitting in Nis that his case be transferred from there to his place of residence? Isn't that -- is that not a right available to him?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: He may file a motion, but it is mainly the prosecutor who files motions on such issues, or maybe the court, which has the case in its hands. The court may say that it does not have the necessary prerequisites to try the case and may ask the Supreme Court of Serbia to decide to which court to delegate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I want to next ask you about Exhibit P2826, which was tab 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I understood that at the start of the session we were having some trouble with e-court. I don't know if you will be able to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's now resolved, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is the document that's entitled "Information about the work of judicial organs in the time of war." You explained to us that this was dated the 12th of May, 1999. That's the date on the last page. And that's the number 12 -- the date 12 September 1999 is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is a document that you prepared?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: On -- on the copy I have, General, unlike many other military documents in this court, I -- I see no signature and there's no stamp that we see on most of those documents. Can you tell us why that is? Is this a draft or is this the final copy that was sent to the Supreme Command?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: That's the final version. When it was drafted, I submitted it to General Matovic in the department for mobilisation, reinforcement and systemic issues, and he was supposed to submit this brief with the accompanying enactment to the Supreme Command Staff, because I as chief of department cannot go directly to the Supreme Command Staff. I have to go through my superior command. And this short brief was revised a bit, and it went from the department from -- for mobilisation and reinforcement and it was used as a basis for changes to units and lower commands. And you must have the version signed by Risto Matovic that went to lower levels. So this is the same thing without a signature. It is not a significant shortcoming legally and formally speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's not a shortcoming to have no signature and -- and no stamp on the document?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
