utterances.text: But there is an indication of the institution which drafted it, and that is quite sufficient, because this same data is used later on and the department for mobilisation, reinforcement and systemic issues uses this information and supplies it together with its accompanying document to the Supreme Command Staff and to lower levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Have you seen the final official version that you say General Matovic forwarded on?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: No. This is the final version, and there is only the cover letter that was signed by General Matovic. That letter is signed. It is logged in, and that cover letter comes with this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understood your earlier answer to indicate that there were some minor revisions. Do you know what changes were made?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, revisions, yes, in the sense that the tasks and the proposed measures that should be taken at a level of the Supreme Command Staff or army level. This is not something that I can state. The administration for reinforcements and mobilisation is the proper organ. General Matovic and -- those corrections were made, and it was indicated there that this report was sent on behalf of the administration for mobilisation, reinforcements, and systematic issues, not on behalf of the legal department. That's why I couldn't sign it, because it was sent from the administration and at the head of that administration was General Matovic, and that is why the cover letter was there, to meet those formal requirements. So the corrections were really minor, and they went in this direction to give greater weight to this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we go to page 2 of both the English and the B/C/S. General, when Mr. Sepenuk was asking you questions under item 2.3 in the -- regarding the 3rd Army, in the second paragraph you indicated to us that there was an error in the last word in the second paragraph and that it should refer to the military district in Pristina rather than Nis; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's the last part of the sentence. It's "the command of the military district in Nis," and it should read "Pristina," because we have the military district in Nis reference -- referred to in the previous text and the one in Nis worked fine, unlike the one in Pristina. So this is just a typo, and that went unnoticed. That's the essence, because linguistically speaking, this just doesn't make any sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I agree. Do you know if it was changed in the final version that General Matovic sent on?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: No. This is the version that went out.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Attached to his separate cover letter.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. In the next paragraph you mention that in their work, very complex criminal cases that deal with serious crimes. And you mentioned terrorism. Judge Bonomy asked you about the military court's jurisdiction over terrorism cases. During -- between April and June of 1999, were the military courts prosecuting any cases of terrorism, for example, against captured KLA members or other individuals who had tried to carry out terrorist acts against the VJ?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, I did not get any such information. I don't think that there were any such cases. Perhaps they were in the pre-criminal procedure stage, but there were no such cases that were already in the judicial stage. There were terrorist acts, but the perpetrators were not captured. And in order to try somebody, to prosecute somebody, you need to have that person. I don't have that information. I'm not aware of it. Perhaps there were such cases, but I didn't hear of any of them in the reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Why did you include that phrase about terrorism, then, to show that the military judicial organs attached to the Pristina Corps command had encountered these complex criminal cases dealing with serious crimes? It doesn't sound like terrorism was taking much of their time or expertise.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: I did give an example. There were such cases. They encountered such acts but were unable to prosecute them. So this is why I put it here. I gave you an example, when terrorist groups kidnapped two soldiers and an officer who had come to the courthouse on that day, and after being examined before the court as witnesses, they were to go back to their units but they were abducted on the way back and their fate remains unknown. All the relevant organs took measures to investigate this, but it was impossible. During the war, in Kosovo and Metohija, as far as I can remember, about 30 members of the army are still missing. They were not killed in action. They had been abducted, and their fate remains unknown. So these are the acts of terrorism and the judicial organs encountered that kind of difficulties. This is why this is included in this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In your statistics for the -- the cases that were done by the military judicial organs, where would a -- a crime involving terrorism be listed? Would that be among the statistics for other crimes?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it could be in the other crimes rubric, but I cannot really tell you whether any such proceedings were conducted and whether the indicted persons were actually prosecuted, because they were unknown and until you catch the perpetrator, you don't know who it is, so these are unidentified perpetrators and you are not likely to find those in any of the reports that we had in our file, and it's impossible to go and look for them in the other crimes, because you have to prosecute an identified person with a full name. You cannot prosecute an unidentified perpetrator. And those acts of terrorism, we couldn't identify the perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Are you -- did you ever see a -- a report from General -- Colonel -- General Delic's 549th Brigade about prosecutions in his area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, I didn't get anything like that from him, and he was not duty-bound to do so. I got my reports from the courts, not from the units.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And during the state of war, could KLA -- say, captured KLA be prosecuted in civilian courts, or only in the military courts?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Before military courts, if the military personnel was targeted. If the MUP units were targeted, then this was in the jurisdiction of civilian courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In item 2.4, you're talking about the Navy, and I'm reading from the second sentence. It says: "Even though they have not had a large number of cases, three judges openly stated that they would not act on criminal cases, using as their excuse that their safety, personal security, and jobs were not guaranteed ...." Do you know why they felt that their personal security and jobs were not guaranteed if they were to handle criminal cases?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: I know about this circumstance, because the Republic of Montenegro, its government, once the state of war was declared, instead of making it possible for the conscripts to be mobilised into their wartime units, they, contrary to the needs, proclaimed the universal work obligation, which meant that all the conscripts that had to go to the units, they were picked up and they were assigned to work units. And there was no need whatsoever for those work units. So those work units exist under the law on defence. You have to mobilise people in order for -- to supply the needs of the defence industry and so on. But this is the way in which they tried to go around the mobilisation call, but the judges who responded to the mobilisation call, they received threats and the judges found themselves between the rock and the hard place, whether to respond to the call-up and to perform his duties as a mobilised person and then face being fired because he went against a decision of the government. So these were the situations that we're talking about here. Some judges who actually did work in the military court, they were fired from their courts where they actually were employed. This was a violation of the law, but the republican organs did that. Unfortunately, it's a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we go to the next page in both languages. And in item number 4, General, you were talking about basic problems. Yes, the second paragraph: "There is a slight increase in more complex crime, with an increasing number of perpetrators committing serious crimes ...." Was this increase -- was this noticed increase in crimes a result of better reporting or reporting of crimes that had happened earlier, or was it a result of new and additional crimes being committed at the time you were writing this in May of 1999, or is it some combination of those two things?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, all those factors existed. Such an assessment can only be made on the basis of the data one receives, on the basis of the number of persons against whom criminal reports were filed. But then once the court proceedings began -- begin, then we have the qualification of the act. We have the number of perpetrators that took part in the combination of the criminal acts. You can see that from the overview, where you can see the number of participants. Then on the basis of these data, you can conclude that we have a larger number of perpetrators, with more serious crimes. So we have better reporting and we have the fact that the court proceedings were instituted -- were speeded up on a fast track. So we cannot really rule out any of these factors. If you have a crime that is not detected, then this crime doesn't exist for the person compiling a report. So only when a case comes to the prosecutor, once the proceedings are initiated, then you get the data about the crimes and the perpetrators. And you can ascertain that there are several perpetrators who committed one and the same act. And this is what is actually presented here in a single sentence, to make it clear in a nutshell so appropriate measures could be taken, first of all, to prevent any such increases and also to detect any crimes that have already been committed as soon as possible, because if a crime is detected and if a criminal proceedings are instituted, that acts as a deterrent.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you here. I think you've answered my question. The next question relates to that. You say "there is a slight increase in more complex crime." What's your definition of "more complex crime"? What were you talking about there?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we're talking about more serious crimes that involve several participants or perpetrators. They are more difficult to detect because people tried to cover up. And these are the factors that make those crimes more complex. So they are more serious in the manner of their perpetration. We have several perpetrators. The consequences are more severe. Evidence is being eliminated. This makes it more difficult to detect such crimes and to prosecute them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can we go to the next page. And, General, I want to ask you about Article number 6,"Proposed measures." You mentioned in item 6.1, number 4: "Compile fortnightly reports on the work of military judicial organs and send them to the unit commands." Do you know, was -- was that done? Was that implemented?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And we actually set a tighter deadline at -- at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know where those reports would be found today?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Those reports have to be in the archive. Reports were made and data were then distributed to the lower commands. Excerpts were made and were sent to the relevant units. They contained data that were relevant for those units.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Would this be in the archives of the legal administration?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: This is all in the central archive.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can we go, then, to the last item, 6.3, "For units and organs at other levels." Number 2 says: "When military judicial organs prosecute, they must give priority in their work, within the law and their competencies, to cases where the perpetrators have a higher level of education and are in responsible positions in the Yugoslav Army or society." In your report, can you tell us how many officers were prosecuted for crimes against life and limb?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the information is in here. I can't give you the figures off the top of my head. There were not many of them, but there were such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, on one of -- we'll have to look at it tomorrow, but on one of the -- one of the charts I'd seen, it did have a breakdown by rank for the various categories of crime. And I think the total number for life and limb crimes and -- and the one I'm thinking of was somewhere in the neighbourhood of 32 or 34 individuals. There might have been one non-commissioned officer and all the rest were privates or reservists. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, if it is contained in the overview, then it's correct for that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, can we break for the day? I'll have to show him that chart tomorrow. I'm sorry, I have about 30 minutes, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Gojovic, we have to terminate the proceedings for the day at this stage, since there will be another case in this courtroom in the afternoon. That means that you will have to come back tomorrow to complete your evidence, and that will be at 9.00 tomorrow morning. Between now and then, as I'm sure you're very much aware, it's vital that you should have no discussion with anyone about the evidence in this case, any part of the evidence. Please confine your communications with other people to matters other than the evidence in this case. Now please leave the courtroom with the usher, and we shall see you at 9.00 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 3rd day of October, 2007, at 9.00 a.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24
